vulnerabilities.name: Missing Anti-clickjacking Header
vulnerabilities.description: The response does not protect against 'ClickJacking' attacks. It should include either Content-Security-Policy with 'frame-ancestors' directive or X-Frame-Options.
vulnerabilities.solution:
Modern Web browsers support the Content-Security-Policy and X-Frame-Options HTTP headers. Ensure one of them is set on all web pages returned by your site/app.
If you expect the page to be framed only by pages on your server (e.g. it's part of a FRAMESET) then you'll want to use SAMEORIGIN, otherwise if you never expect the page to be framed, you should use DENY. Alternatively consider implementing Content Security Policy's "frame-ancestors" directive.

vulnerabilities.name: Content Security Policy (CSP) Header Not Set
vulnerabilities.description: Content Security Policy (CSP) is an added layer of security that helps to detect and mitigate certain types of attacks, including Cross Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks. These attacks are used for everything from data theft to site defacement or distribution of malware. CSP provides a set of standard HTTP headers that allow website owners to declare approved sources of content that browsers should be allowed to load on that page — covered types are JavaScript, CSS, HTML frames, fonts, images and embeddable objects such as Java applets, ActiveX, audio and video files.
vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is configured to set the Content-Security-Policy header.

vulnerabilities.name: X-Content-Type-Options Header Missing
vulnerabilities.description: The Anti-MIME-Sniffing header X-Content-Type-Options was not set to 'nosniff'. This allows older versions of Internet Explorer and Chrome to perform MIME-sniffing on the response body, potentially causing the response body to be interpreted and displayed as a content type other than the declared content type. Current (early 2014) and legacy versions of Firefox will use the declared content type (if one is set), rather than performing MIME-sniffing.
vulnerabilities.solution:
Ensure that the application/web server sets the Content-Type header appropriately, and that it sets the X-Content-Type-Options header to 'nosniff' for all web pages.
If possible, ensure that the end user uses a standards-compliant and modern web browser that does not perform MIME-sniffing at all, or that can be directed by the web application/web server to not perform MIME-sniffing.

ai_analysis.simplified_description: This vulnerability means that your web page can be embedded in a frame by other sites, which can trick users into clicking on something different than they intended. This is called clickjacking.
ai_analysis.impact: An attacker could trick users into performing actions on your site without their knowledge, potentially leading to unauthorized actions.
remediation_steps: Add the X-Frame-Options header to your HTTP response to prevent your site from being framed.
Alternatively, use the Content-Security-Policy header with the 'frame-ancestors' directive.

ai_analysis.original_name: Content Security Policy (CSP) Header Not Set
ai_analysis.simplified_description: This means your site does not have a Content Security Policy, which helps prevent attacks like Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) by controlling what resources can be loaded.
ai_analysis.impact: Without a CSP, your site is more vulnerable to XSS attacks, which can lead to data theft or site defacement.
remediation_steps: Configure your web server to include a Content-Security-Policy header.
Define the sources of content that are allowed to be loaded on your site.

ai_analysis.simplified_description: This means your server is not telling browsers to avoid MIME-sniffing, which can lead to security issues if a browser misinterprets the content type.
ai_analysis.impact: An attacker could exploit this to serve malicious content disguised as a different type, leading to potential data breaches.
remediation_steps: Set the X-Content-Type-Options header to 'nosniff' in your server configuration.
Ensure that the Content-Type header is set correctly for all responses.

ai_analysis.simplified_description: Your server is revealing information about the technology stack it uses, which can help attackers identify potential vulnerabilities.
ai_analysis.impact: An attacker could use this information to target specific vulnerabilities in the technologies your server uses.
remediation_steps: Configure your web server to suppress the 'X-Powered-By' header.
Review your server settings to ensure no sensitive information is exposed.

vulnerabilities.name: Missing Anti-clickjacking Header
vulnerabilities.description: The response does not protect against 'ClickJacking' attacks. It should include either Content-Security-Policy with 'frame-ancestors' directive or X-Frame-Options.
vulnerabilities.solution:
Modern Web browsers support the Content-Security-Policy and X-Frame-Options HTTP headers. Ensure one of them is set on all web pages returned by your site/app.
If you expect the page to be framed only by pages on your server (e.g. it's part of a FRAMESET) then you'll want to use SAMEORIGIN, otherwise if you never expect the page to be framed, you should use DENY. Alternatively consider implementing Content Security Policy's "frame-ancestors" directive.

This allows older versions of Internet Explorer and Chrome to perform MIME-sniffing on the response body, potentially causing the response body to be interpreted and displayed as a content type other than the declared content type. Current (early 2014) and legacy versions of Firefox will use the declared content type (if one is set), rather than performing MIME-sniffing.
vulnerabilities.solution:
Ensure that the application/web server sets the Content-Type header appropriately, and that it sets the X-Content-Type-Options header to 'nosniff' for all web pages.
If possible, ensure that the end user uses a standards-compliant and modern web browser that does not perform MIME-sniffing at all, or that can be directed by the web application/web server to not perform MIME-sniffing.

vulnerabilities.description: The Anti-MIME-Sniffing header X-Content-Type-Options was not set to 'nosniff'. This allows older versions of Internet Explorer and Chrome to perform MIME-sniffing on the response body, potentially causing the response body to be interpreted and displayed as a content type other than the declared content type. Current (early 2014) and legacy versions of Firefox will use the declared content type (if one is set), rather than performing MIME-sniffing.
vulnerabilities.solution:
Ensure that the application/web server sets the Content-Type header appropriately, and that it sets the X-Content-Type-Options header to 'nosniff' for all web pages.
If possible, ensure that the end user uses a standards-compliant and modern web browser that does not perform MIME-sniffing at all, or that can be directed by the web application/web server to not perform MIME-sniffing.

ai_analysis.simplified_description: This vulnerability means that your web page can be embedded in a frame by other sites, which can trick users into clicking on something different than they think. This is called Clickjacking.
ai_analysis.impact: An attacker could trick users into performing actions on your site without their knowledge, potentially leading to unauthorized actions.
remediation_steps: Add the X-Frame-Options header to your HTTP response.
Alternatively, implement a Content-Security-Policy header with the 'frame-ancestors' directive.

ai_analysis.original_name: Content Security Policy (CSP) Header Not Set
ai_analysis.simplified_description: This means your site doesn't have a Content Security Policy, which helps prevent attacks like Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) by controlling what resources can be loaded.
ai_analysis.impact: Without a CSP, your site is more vulnerable to XSS attacks, which can lead to data theft or site defacement.
remediation_steps: Configure your web server to include a Content-Security-Policy header.
Define the sources of content that are allowed to be loaded.

ai_analysis.simplified_description: This means your server is not telling browsers to avoid MIME-sniffing, which can lead to security issues if the content type is misinterpreted.
ai_analysis.impact: An attacker could exploit this to serve malicious content disguised as a different type, potentially leading to data breaches.
remediation_steps: Set the X-Content-Type-Options header to 'nosniff' in your server configuration.
Ensure that the Content-Type header is correctly set for all responses.

ai_analysis.original_name: Server Leaks Information via "X-Powered-By" HTTP Response Header Field(s)
ai_analysis.simplified_description: Your server is revealing its technology stack through the 'X-Powered-By' header, which can help attackers identify potential vulnerabilities.
ai_analysis.impact: An attacker could use this information to target known vulnerabilities in the disclosed technology.
remediation_steps: Remove the 'X-Powered-By' header from your server's HTTP responses.
Configure your web server to suppress this header.

summary: The scan identified 4 real vulnerabilities with an overall risk level of Medium. Immediate attention is required to address the missing security headers to enhance the application's security posture.

vulnerabilities.name: Missing Anti-clickjacking Header
vulnerabilities.description: The response does not protect against 'ClickJacking' attacks. It should include either Content-Security-Policy with 'frame-ancestors' directive or X-Frame-Options.
vulnerabilities.solution:
Modern Web browsers support the Content-Security-Policy and X-Frame-Options HTTP headers. Ensure one of them is set on all web pages returned by your site/app.
If you expect the page to be framed only by pages on your server (e.g. it's part of a FRAMESET) then you'll want to use SAMEORIGIN, otherwise if you never expect the page to be framed, you should use DENY. Alternatively consider implementing Content Security Policy's "frame-ancestors" directive.

vulnerabilities.name: Content Security Policy (CSP) Header Not Set
vulnerabilities.description: Content Security Policy (CSP) is an added layer of security that helps to detect and mitigate certain types of attacks, including Cross Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks. These attacks are used for everything from data theft to site defacement or distribution of malware. CSP provides a set of standard HTTP headers that allow website owners to declare approved sources of content that browsers should be allowed to load on that page — covered types are JavaScript, CSS, HTML frames, fonts, images and embeddable objects such as Java applets, ActiveX, audio and video files.
vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is configured to set the Content-Security-Policy header.

vulnerabilities.name: Cross-Domain Misconfiguration
vulnerabilities.description: Web browser data loading may be possible, due to a Cross Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) misconfiguration on the web server.
vulnerabilities.solution:
Ensure that sensitive data is not available in an unauthenticated manner (using IP address white-listing, for instance).
Configure the "Access-Control-Allow-Origin" HTTP header to a more restrictive set of domains, or remove all CORS headers entirely, to allow the web browser to enforce the Same Origin Policy (SOP) in a more restrictive manner.

Modern Web browsers support the Content-Security-Policy and X-Frame-Options HTTP headers. Ensure one of them is set on all web pages returned by your site/app.

remediation_steps: Add the X-Frame-Options header to your HTTP response to prevent your site from being framed.
Alternatively, implement a Content-Security-Policy header with the 'frame-ancestors' directive.

ai_analysis.simplified_description: Not having a Content Security Policy means your site is more vulnerable to attacks like Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), where attackers can inject malicious scripts.
ai_analysis.impact: Without CSP, attackers can execute scripts that steal user data or manipulate the site.
remediation_steps: Configure your web server to include a Content-Security-Policy header.
Define the sources of content that are allowed to be loaded on your site.

ai_analysis.simplified_description: This vulnerability indicates that your server allows requests from any domain, which can expose sensitive data to unauthorized sites.
ai_analysis.impact: An attacker could exploit this to access sensitive data or perform actions on behalf of users.

Consider removing CORS headers if they are not needed.

Use generic information instead of specific version details.

vulnerabilities.name: Missing Anti-clickjacking Header
vulnerabilities.description: The response does not protect against 'ClickJacking' attacks. It should include either Content-Security-Policy with 'frame-ancestors' directive or X-Frame-Options.
vulnerabilities.solution:
Modern Web browsers support the Content-Security-Policy and X-Frame-Options HTTP headers. Ensure one of them is set on all web pages returned by your site/app.
If you expect the page to be framed only by pages on your server (e.g. it's part of a FRAMESET) then you'll want to use SAMEORIGIN, otherwise if you never expect the page to be framed, you should use DENY. Alternatively consider implementing Content Security Policy's "frame-ancestors" directive.

vulnerabilities.name: Content Security Policy (CSP) Header Not Set
vulnerabilities.description: Content Security Policy (CSP) is an added layer of security that helps to detect and mitigate certain types of attacks, including Cross Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks. These attacks are used for everything from data theft to site defacement or distribution of malware. CSP provides a set of standard HTTP headers that allow website owners to declare approved sources of content that browsers should be allowed to load on that page — covered types are JavaScript, CSS, HTML frames, fonts, images and embeddable objects such as Java applets, ActiveX, audio and video files.
vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is configured to set the Content-Security-Policy header.

vulnerabilities.name: Cross-Domain Misconfiguration
vulnerabilities.description: Web browser data loading may be possible, due to a Cross Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) misconfiguration on the web server.
vulnerabilities.solution:
Ensure that sensitive data is not available in an unauthenticated manner (using IP address white-listing, for instance).
Configure the "Access-Control-Allow-Origin" HTTP header to a more restrictive set of domains, or remove all CORS headers entirely, to allow the web browser to enforce the Same Origin Policy (SOP) in a more restrictive manner.

vulnerabilities.name: X-Content-Type-Options Header Missing
vulnerabilities.description: The Anti-MIME-Sniffing header X-Content-Type-Options was not set to 'nosniff'. This allows older versions of Internet Explorer and Chrome to perform MIME-sniffing on the response body, potentially causing the response body to be interpreted and displayed as a content type other than the declared content type. Current (early 2014) and legacy versions of Firefox will use the declared content type (if one is set), rather than performing MIME-sniffing.

Ensure that the application/web server sets the Content-Type header appropriately, and that it sets the X-Content-Type-Options header to 'nosniff' for all web pages.
If possible, ensure that the end user uses a standards-compliant and modern web browser that does not perform MIME-sniffing at all, or that can be directed by the web application/web server to not perform MIME-sniffing.

vulnerabilities.name: X-Content-Type-Options Header Missing
vulnerabilities.description: The Anti-MIME-Sniffing header X-Content-Type-Options was not set to 'nosniff'. This allows older versions of Internet Explorer and Chrome to perform MIME-sniffing on the response body, potentially causing the response body to be interpreted and displayed as a content type other than the declared content type. Current (early 2014) and legacy versions of Firefox will use the declared content type (if one is set), rather than performing MIME-sniffing.
vulnerabilities.solution:
Ensure that the application/web server sets the Content-Type header appropriately, and that it sets the X-Content-Type-Options header to 'nosniff' for all web pages.
If possible, ensure that the end user uses a standards-compliant and modern web browser that does not perform MIME-sniffing at all, or that can be directed by the web application/web server to not perform MIME-sniffing.
